On schedule I.
Customs tariff-87. Vegetables, fresh, in their natural state: asparagus, green beans, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, carrots, beets, n.o.p., cauliflower, egg-plant, celery, cucumbers, lettuce, parsley, green peas, rhubarb, spinach, tomatoes, watercress, whitloof, endive, and fresh vegetables, n.o.p.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I have not taken any part in this debate, but now I want to ask the minister a question. I am not particularly worried whether Toronto or Moose Jaw can secure celery or lettuce or some of these other things right now, but the people of my riding are particularly interested in whether they are going to be protected from dumping if they grow these vegetables and fruits. This matter has been brought up already by some Ontario members, and I believe by the hon. member for Kamloops. We all know what has happened in the past, under all governments. Pears, for instance have been brought into Canada in order to keep up prices in Washington. Peaches have been dumped in our province for the same reason. As far as the minister can give us an assurance, we would like to know that this will not be permitted in future. We would also be interested if the minister could give us some idea of the length of time we will continue under the present program. In British Columbia we can produce all the cabbages necessary for the whole of Canada, but that will require expensive equipment, such as sprayers, planting machines, and so on. We cannot go to that expense unless we are sure how long the program will last. So I should like to know just how far the minister can go
on behalf of the government in giving us an outline of the situation at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
As the committee knows, a number of hon. members have raised this question and have asked whether I could give any assurance as to the length of time during which these restrictions are likely to be in force. The hon. member for Fraser Valley discussed that question with me, and I have been giving a good deal of thought to it. As I have said on other occasions, these import restrictions on fresh fruits and vegetables are intended to be temporary. They are put on as a necessary measure to conserve exchange, and the government would not feel justified in continuing them beyond the period of time when our exchange position makes it necessary. Therefore it is the policy of the government to relax and remove the restrictions as soon as the exchange position justifies that action. In other words the government is not prepared to retain these measures indefinitely as a protection to the fruit and vegetable industry. The permanent and continuing degree of protection to the industry is provided. of course, in the existing customs tariff.
I realize, however, that the growers of these fruits and vegetables are placed in a difficult position with respect to planning increases in production; and while I am conscious of the risks and dangers of trying to make predictions, as I said before, I think I can go this far. As I now see the situation and as I now view the prospects of our exchange position I think it is highly improbable that a complete removal of these restrictions with respect to fresh fruits and vegetables will occur much before the end of this calendar year, and it may be that some degree of restriction will continue into the early part of 1949. As far as possible it would be the government's intention not to remove or relax these import controls at a time when that action would have serious or disastrous effects on the marketing of Canadian produce. But I cannot bind the government to any unconditional guarantee that no produce grown in Canada in 1948 will have to face any competition from imported goods. As I said nearly three months ago, the government intends to relax restrictions on basic or essential items such as cabbages, carrots, potatoes and onions when it becomes clear that Canadian supplies are nearing exhaustion.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
May I ask the minister why our Canadian growers of vegetables cannot compete successfully with United States growers without tariff protection?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I wish to make it perfectly clear that the farmers of the Fraser valley can compete. We do not want protection; but neither do we want dumping in our province.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: One of the reasons we feel we cannot compete is that in the country to the south of us on account of climatic conditions they can grow two or three crops. I know of districts where they are growing three crops of vegetables each year. Crop after crop is taken off; because of the warm weather and irrigation facilities the people in those areas can grow those crops and flood our market. That is one of the reasons why we in British Columbia cannot compete.

On numerous occasions hon. members on this side of the house have asked the minister for a statement as to how long these restrictions are to be kept on. But the moment a back bencher from his own party gets up the minister is only too pleased to reply, and to supply the information. Total imports from the United States entered for consumption in Canada during that period were valued at $1,953,742,000. Exports of Canadian produce during the same period were valued at $1,008,494,457 and exports of foreign produce at $22,500,000. If we subtract the total of exports from the total of imports we find that the unfavourable balance of trade with the United States during the twelve months ended October 31, 1947, was $942 million odd. The unfavourable balance in respect of vegetables is only $12,000,000, a small amount compared with the total unfavourable balance. The largest import item is tomatoes, which totalled $3,601,767. The next is lettuce, $2,931,168; then celery, $2,453,501 and then

potatoes, n.o.p., which I assume would cover fresh potatoes, $1,182,181. Then the next item is carrots, $1,228,252.
During the war we were told to eat more vegetables. Considerable propaganda was put out to the effect that we should eat more vegetables, that they were good for health. They were recommended for the young and the old. The production of vegetables is not an easy matter in most parts of this country during a large part of the year and therefore we have to import from the United States. Vegetables are necessary to provide a well balanced diet, and I do not see why we should deprive ourselves of these vegetables from the south when they are supposed to be so good for all. It would not interfere with the farmers to permit them to come in. At the present time farmers do pretty well with the production of vegetables. They have their own markets and many of them can vegetables during the summer for consumption during the hard months of the year. Does it mean that simply because these items have been included it is impossible to change them? If it is impossible to change them, why discuss them?
I know the minister is a reasonable man and if something is submitted to him it may be possible to convince him that it should be changed. If, as the minister has said, this is a temporary measure, why does he insist on keeping it in force? The result will be that farmers in some parts of the country will try to raise these vegetables. If the minister was in earnest when he said that this measure was temporary then those people will be greatly disappointed when the legislation is no longer in force. They think that they will have the Canadian market during the winter, but there are some difficulties in their path.
One difficulty in having fresh vegetables grown in British Columbia sold in the east during the winter is the high air freight rates. If those vegetables could be sent to the east in refrigerator cars where they would be kept in good condition at ordinary freight rates, it would be possible for the farmers of British Columbia to increase their production of fresh vegetables. We in the east know how delicious are the apples of British Columbia during the winter, but they are most expensive. There again it is a question of freight rates.
Is it necessary to insist so much on a matter which could be settled amicably and would be for the benefit of the country? It seems to me that it should be possible to convince our farmers in a reasonable and commonsense way that this is a condition which has existed
for a long time; that it will not ruin the country to bring in vegetables from the United States to an amount of nearly $17,000,000 when we export vegetables to that country to an amount of nearly $5,000,000.
Someone said that the $180,000,000 which would be needed for Newfoundland was just peanuts. The amount involved in the importation of vegetables is around $15,000,000, only about one-twelfth the amount. I hope the minister will reconsider this matter. If we are to go through a period of austerity I would recall to him that those who take the vows of poverty exist on a vegetarian diet. They are austere people. We see them going around barefooted asking for alms. They live on vegetables because vegetables are the food of the poor. Why not let these vegetables come in? It would involve an amount which is trifling when compared with the unfavourable balance of trade with the United States. Besides that it would be good for the health of the Canadian people.
I am not going to press the matter further. I have given these figures in the hope that the minister will understand. I am quite sure he does. It is possible to disagree with him at times and have good reasons for doing so. It is possible to improve this bill and that is why it is before the committee. I agree entirely with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
This is not a party question. It is not a case of one group gaining a victory over the minister. It is simply a discussion by plain men who want to make the best of it. If we have to wait until the farmers in other parts of Canada are able to produce the vegetables we are now importing we shall have nothing in the meantime. I cannot understand this austerity when we cannot eat vegetables although all the store counters are loaded with candies, chocolates, fancy biscuits, and the like. I leave it to the minister in the hope that he will make the right decision in the matter.

There is one sad feature about this; it was the necessity for conserving United States dollar exchange that brought this matter to the attention of the government. They are prohibiting this literature from entry into Canada, not particularly because it is undesirable but because they need United States dollars. That is the sad thing. But I commend the minister's action because I believe the government has some responsibility with respect to the morals of this country. I have often heard it said that when it conies to morals it is the responsibility of the home, the school and the church. But you cannot tag on to the home, the school and the church the responsibility of keeping undesirable literature out of this country. I have never yet known a home that has deliberately subscribed to certain types of comic magazines, sex stories, or photogravure literature, for the purpose of bettering the home. I have never known a school or church to have its library packed with that sort of literature. If anything, they want to keep it out. The only authorities who can do this happen to be governmental authorities. Recently I have been quite alarmed at the tremendous flood of certain types of pulp magazines, story books and comics that have been on sale on most of our news stands. They seem to have multiplied in recent years. My own boy likes to read the comics; and as a matter of fact I have no objection to good, wholesome comic magazines. As I said before, I do not wish to enter into that discussion, nor shall I do so. But I am concerned with the fact that censorship ought to be efficient. I do not believe the various customs officers stationed at different points across the country are qualified to deal with this matter, nor could we expect them to be so qualified. I do know that in cases of doubt the material is sent to a central point where a man who has the ultimate responsibility must make a decision with respect to it. I did say, however, that the gentleman who had that responsibility during the last session of parliament was not as efficient as he should have been.
I am almost in total agreement with what the hon. member has just said with respect to pornographic material. But I must point out that, on the other hand, I believe many legitimate books are refused entry into this country because of the ignorance of the people who have the censoring of them. There is a great difference between certain novels and certain books which, through their very nature, if they are to be true to life, are bound to be realistic. There is a difference, however between the genuinely written and realistic novel and one that is deliberately pornographic for the purpose of making sales, by appealing to depraved tastes. I believe that inefficiency in censorship works both ways. Not only does it allow to come in material which should be kept out, but it also keeps out much material which should be allowed to come in.

I have been so much interested in the remarks just made that I should like to add one further word. We all recognize that censorship is a very difficult procedure. It has to be handled wisely, because we must recognize that there is an infinite variety of opinions in the matter. But I do not believe there are two opinions in the house as to what we find when we go to some of the public newsstands. When we see what is in them we know that the system is wrong, and that it must have an evil influence. If any good can

come out of this evil bill, or if this can possibly be the occasion of setting up some system-and it has to be a wise system, not rigid and unthinking; I recognize that-I should hope it might come now. However, a large number of corner stores in all cities have been making a living from selling literature of this kind. I made an investigation by calling on about ten cigar stores which have been selling this type of literature. I asked them what the prohibition of the importation of such literature as they had on their shelves would do to their businesses. The usual answer was that they made about $25 a week from the sale of it, and they felt that the prohibition would hit them pretty hard.
What have we to offer in place of the literature on the prohibited list? Can anything be done to encourage the importation of better literature from the old country so that the cigar stores on the corner may continue to make a living? If we prevent their selling this kind of reading material-a procedure with which we agree-is there any effort made to give something in its place so that they will be able to continue to make a living? After all, $25 is an important item to a small cigar store.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I have a case in mind of a man who spent considerable money in September, 1946, to arrange for the sole agency for the importation of Christmas cards from a high-class gallery. This man has spent a good deal of money in working up business, but now these cards are banned from Great Britain. His order may not amount to more than $10,000, but that would help to pay for some of the wheat that Great Britain is buying from us. This man is a veteran of the first war, an amputation case. He has the agency for one line of goods from Great Britain which he can still bring in, but the one line is not sufficient. If he were permitted to bring in the two lines he could make a living out of it and pay his overhead. If these high-class Christmas cards are banned he will have to fold up the other business. Customs tariff-415a. Refrigerators, domestic or store, completely equipped or not.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
We had a discussion on section 3 of the bill, and I believe the minister admitted that as regards oil burning refrigerators there was discrimination against certain groups in the country who could not obtain automatic refrigeration from any other source. Since that time, I have made further inquiries
and I find that refrigerators of this particular type are not made in the soft-currency countries. As a matter of fact, I believe there is one firm making them in the United States. Previously there had been three firms engaged in the business; but since it is a more or less diminishing business and as electricity becomes more widely distributed, refrigerators of this type are not used. There is no chance whatever of a branch factory being established in Canada. Under these circumstances I think there is a good case for leniency on the part of the minister in this matter of allowing this particular type of refrigerator into Canada. Farmers are not the only ones affected. There are a large number of tourist and other camps throughout Canada where other types of refrigerators are expensive or difficult to obtain. I am, therefore, going to move that this item 415a be amended by adding after the word "not" the following words: "but not including
oil-burning refrigerators". That is seconded by Mr. Nicholson. I think the minister might give some serious consideration to this matter. I do not think it involves a large expenditure of United States dollars, but I believe it means a great deal to people living in areas where electricity is not available.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The other evening I promised my hon. friend that I would look into the whole situation and give it sympathetic consideration. That undertaking still stands. I am afraid that I cannot agree to the removal of the prohibition. After I have looked into the matter, it may be well that we could place it under a reasonable quota; but I do not think the entry of this type of refrigerator should be completely without restriction. For that reason and for that reason alone, I cannot now accept the amendment which is made. But I will give it consideration and see if they can be transferred to the quota list.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I would be prepared to withdraw my amendment if the minister is prepared to say they will be placed under quota.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I cannot give that undertaking. I cannot say what the importations are or what it involves in terms of United States dollars. That is my test in regard to these matters. The responsibility I have is to see that our already dangerously low reserves of United States dollars are conserved. Until I am satisfied that I can justify allowing items of this kind in, and know to what extent it can be done, I do not want to give a formal undertaking. The most I can say is, as I said to my hon. friend the other night, that I will give the matter careful and sympathetic consideration.

Foreign Exchange Conservation

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I understand that certain United States washing machine companies have branches in Canada. If this bill goes through, does it mean that those branches will not be able to get washing machines under any circumstances?

[Mr. Abbott.l
near the supply to meet the demand. My point was that apparently some of these branches will have to close up, and there are veterans and others who have started up agencies with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

Mr. LOW": The minister would not hesitate, would he, to allow sewing machines in from the LTnited Kingdom in case we found ourselves short in Canada?

speechtext: (Comox-Alberni): It is also possible that a commercial vessel might be bought over there and converted to a pleasure craft here. I should think a great deal of discretion would have to be given the authorities.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I want to point out to the minister that these can be manufactured and at present are being manufactured in the soft currency countries. Customs tariff-234. Perfumery, including toilet preparations, non-alcoholic, viz., hair oils, tooth and other powders and washes, pomatums, pastes and all other perfumed preparations, n.o.p., used for the hair, mouth or skin.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I should like to thank the minister for holding this item over; I was in a committee meeting elsewhere when it was called. Will the minister consider transferring this item to another schedule, or dealing with it in such a way that it will not prevent the importation of French perfumes into Canada? I have in mind two young veterans of the Canadian armed forces who established themselves in business in Canada as importers of French perfumes, and other similar products such as face powders, hair lotions and brilliantines. I do not know that they are the the only ones who have done this. They had established connections with the French producers of these goods while serving in the forces and are in a position to carry on a business which would be useful in Canada, and would also help the French producers. Supplies of these materials are available in France.
It so happens that the two veterans about whom I am speaking, relying on the hope of establishing a good line of French perfumes, sank into their business all the wealth they had in the world, including their re-establishment grants. Now, with the virtually complete exclusion of French perfumes and similar products, not only are they faced with ruin,

but harm is being done to the good relations they had established with the French producers. This particular case has I believe, been brought to the attention of Mr. Taylor.
The partnership in question had hoped during the current year to import perfumes and other like materials to a value of not less than two million francs, and this is a serious matter for them. I am not speaking about perfumes from the Lhiited States, but rather perfumes from France, and I urge that special consideration be given to a case of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: The committee will notice that this item relates only to non-alcoholic perfumes and preparations. Under this item goods to the value of only $9,000 were imported from France during the base period. Many of the French perfumes are alcoholic, and as such they come under tariff item 160, concerning which there is no prohibition. So that I believe it is fair to say that a substantial portion of the French perfumes are not prohibited.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
There are two observations I should like to make. First, last year's statistics do not apply. These young men are just starting up, and the volume of business they did last year is not to be compared with the volume they had every reason to expect to do this year. Then, as to alcoholic content, I am told that if one wants to transform a non-alcoholic perfume into an alcoholic perfume it can be done by debasing the product through the addition of a portion of alcohol.
However, I do not think the point the minister makes covers this situation. The perfumes to which I am referring, and in the sale of which these young veterans were establishing themselves, are almost entirely non-alcoholic. They do not wish to adulterate their perfumes by the addition of alcohol so that they may be classified as having alcoholic content, simply to evade the provisions of the schedule. They propose to sell well-known and well-established brands of non-alcoholic French perfumes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
The difficulty here, as with other items, is that these non-alcoholic perfumes mostly come from the United States. Last year, over $400,000 worth was imported from the United States, only $8,000 worth from France and something like $70,000 worth from the United Kingdom. Unless we are prepared to revert to the discriminatory principle, we would have to let in a lot of these perfumes from the United States in order to let them in from France. In the case of the more expensire alcoholic perfumes, last year $80,000

Foreign Exchange Conservation
worth was imported from France as against only $6,000 from the United States. I never knew that the high-class perfumes contained alcohol until this debate came on.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I would urge the minister to regard this case as being one of exceptional hardship. This was to be a new business in Canada which would have been good for Canadians and for the French producers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I will look into the circumstances of the case.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: I will look into the circumstances of the particular case.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: It may be that there are not many cases of this kind, but the one I suggest is of such severe hardship that I think the minister might well deal with it as such.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Would the minister mind giving the basis for his conclusion as to the amount of perfumes that might be brought in from France in accordance with the non-discriminatory principle so that we can understand just what he is advocating?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: There are two principal items dealing with perfumes. One is the nonalcoholic type which, I am told, is the cheaper perfume. In that case the major importations were from the United States and not from France. In the case of the more expensive perfumes which apparently contain alcohol, the principal importations were from France, with very little coming from the United States. The figures which I gave for the more expensive alcoholic perfumes were $82,000 from France as against only $6,000 from the United States.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Upon what does the minister base his reasoning in order to determine when importations from France are nondiscriminatory and when they are not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: We tried to take the items which would result in the greatest saving of United States dollars. That is the principle which has been followed.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext: Perhaps I am not making myself clear to the minister. How does the minister decide whether or not importations from any country are discriminatory'? At what point do they become discriminatory?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROHIBITION OF CERTAIN IMPORTS AND PROVISION FOR IMPORT QUOTAS AND PERMITS
speechtext:
I do not know that I am following my hon. friend quite clearly. We
adopt the same principle so far as all countries are concerned. In other words, if we ban a product, it is banned from all countries. In selecting the articles to be banned we endeavoured, as I explained before, to select articles the major source of supply of which was hard currency countries. We endeavoured to let in those articles whose main source of supply was soft currency countries. That is the general principle we endeavoured to follow in selecting the item to go into either schedule I. the prohibited list, schedule II, the quota list, or to be left off entirely.

I understand that a great deal of the imports in category 2, textiles, are really raw materials. I did not take that in at first; I thought they were things which were brought in and sold over the counter. I understand, however, that a very large quantity indeed of these imports are raw materials, and that they are used for further manufacturing. I think that raises an important question. I am advised that, as they are treated now, they are dealt with automatically ; that no regard is taken to the effect on this industry or that industry. While the minister will realize with what pain I suggest that any additional power should be given to his colleague-and perhaps I should preface this by saying the minister has admitted we are in such a mess that all the ordinary rules of sensible conduct have to be thrown overboard -I am seriously asking whether these amounts, which I understand are very large, which come in under category 2 and are dealt with in what is represented to me as an entirely automatic way, really should not be in schedule III, and whether the same considerations the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to use in reference to the items contained therein, that is to say the effect on this industry or that industry, should be taken into account. First of all, I should like to ask the minister if my information is correct, that being in schedule II and being on the quota they will be dealt with by the department which administers them practically in an automatic manner, and that the considerations which I suggest are important will not be taken into account. If that is so, I would ask him whether he does not agree that these other considerations should be applied.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The situation is that all raw cotton and all cotton yarns are free; there is no prohibition. All other textiles are under quota. It is quite true, as my hon. friend suggests, that a very large proportion of these textiles are what might be described as semi-processed. It is also correct to say that the quota is determined more or less automatically, on the basis of imports during the preceding year-it is a dollar quota-and the importer is free to select the particular type of textile he will bring in, within his quota. I mentioned in connection with one of the very broad discretionary powers granted- to me under section 6 of the bill, which I said I was sorry had to be in those broad terms, that one reason was to enable the minister administering schedule II to impose a special condition in connection with any particular quota holder if, for instance, he were using up all his dollar quota to bring in certain luxury products. I think

Foreign Exchange Conservation
I cited chenille bedspreads instead of material for overalls, or that sort of thing. It may be, as my hon. friend suggests, that experience will demonstrate that it would be desirable to transfer some items from schedule II to schedule III. If that is the case, by virtue of an amendment which was put in when the bill was being considered' in committee, at any time we can move any item from schedule II to schedule III. And it is pointed' out to me that most of these fabrics are also sold over the counter as well, in larger and smaller quantities.

Notwithstanding whiat the minister has said as to the powers reserved and what can be done, I suggest that there is an immediate problem of substantial size, and I wonder if it could not be dealt with now by the definite transfer of some of these items, perhaps all that come in as raw or semi-raw material, to schedule III. It is pointed out to me that putting them on a quota works a very great hardship on a considerable number of people who have recently gone into business, and I am assured that, tas in other industries, many of them are returned men.
There is one entirely fortuitous situation which I am told has worked great hardship. It is said that, actually not by law but by custom and practice, there' has been a quota here in Canada for the last six or seven years, and that a good many of the people going into business in these small textile establishments found they could not get supplies here in Canada, because the supply houses in this country had their lists of customers and1 could not take on more; and I am told that these new businesses have had to rely solely on United States supplies. It is quite obvious that if they have been relying solely on United' States supplies a quota of 32 per cent is no good to them.
I am also told-though perhaps this is irrelevant to the immediate argument, but at any rate it is incidental to it, and it is an unfortunate thing-that there has sprung up a mushroom lot of wholesalers who flourished greatly, to my regret, during the war, and who now apparently are reappearing. They are on the quotas. They have worked themselves in as intermediaries and they are to be found again, getting in between and making use of the quotas they had during the war to feather their own nests in these new circumstances. For that reason again I am asking-and I hope there may be others in the house who will be sufficiently interested in this to take part in the argument, if they agree-whether this should not be handled in some different way, because to me it seems that this situa-5849-94
tion will work great hardship on the smaller people, those who were not in business in 1940 or 1941, when the informal Canadian quotas were established. .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am afraid I have not made my point clear.
I	quite realize that to get on the quota under the schedule, the quota which is now being effected by the government, anyone who was in business in June, 1947, is eligible. I am suggesting, however, that there was an effective though informal quota system in effect in Canada prior to 1947. The minister's assistant will know whether or not that is true; but I am assured by competent people that it is the case and for that reason you have this very great hardship on the people who are placed under this strict quota* system. I hope I have made my point, and that the minister will take it seriously; because, as I say, it seems to me that the effect of this quota is something which I do not believe was intended. The effect of it appears to be that it will deal a body blow to a very considerable number of people who are now just getting their feet under them in business. I know that was not intended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The effect of this quota is to put great pressure upon buyers to try to get textile imports from the United Kingdom. That is just what was intended. That is one of the main purposes as to why this quota
Foreign Exchange Conservation

was fixed on its present basis. I have tried to bring that out several times in the course of discussion on the bill.
It is very easy to get textiles in the United States. It is easy to see them. It is easy to see samples and, incidentally, prices have been very attractive. But under existing conditions we are extremely anxious that Canadian importers should see what the British have to offer, and should try to get their textiles in the United Kingdom, as they used to do in 1940. That is why these quotas have been fixed on the basis indicated, or that is largely the reason. We believe that it will now have the effect of putting great pressure upon importers, such as those to whom my hon. friend referred, to scrounge around to see if they cannot get British textiles instead of American. That is the purpose of putting the quota on this basis.
If they cannot get British textiles, then we shall have to see what happens-if they are essential. But we are anxious to have it work as I have suggested, and this has been designed and drawn on that basis, namely, that there should be a real incentive on the textile importers to find out what the British have to sell.
I am not disagreeing with that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know my hon. friend is not.

I wish to make that clear, because my argument was not suggesting necessarily that a single extra dollar's worth of United States goods should come in. However, it was suggested that the basis upon which they are at present allocated seems to be working a great hardship on a great many people. But a different test-a test which the minister agrees will not be applied in the department where it is now being considered, and where it will be dealt with automatically-should be applied, and that is the test of keeping people in business. And that is the test which the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to apply, and which I think the minister will agree is a very desirable test in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is an important point. The British are trying to send us about ten times the yardage they sent us last year in cotton textiles. These quotas are, as I say, designed to enable them, to do that. As I said to the committee the other night, there is no effective quota restriction for the time being so far as British textiles are concerned. There is an extremely effective one so far as United States textiles are concerned. Believe me, if I

were a textiles importer, with these quotas as they are, I Would be scrounging around pretty hard to try to find what British textiles I could get. And that is what we are trying to have them do.

I wish to point out on the strength of the argument I make, that my information is that by reason of this system two manufacturers of overalls have had to close down due to the automatic application of this rule. I suggest that if they were in the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, considering their position-and I am embarrassed when I make this observation; nevertheless I make it -if the Minister of Trade and Commerce were in the position of considering this industry which, presumably, he wishes to keep together, and not only keep it in existence but have it prosper we might reach a very different result indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the position of any textile importer today; any textile importer can get, first, 32 per cent of his United States imports lost year. Second, he can get at least all that he was able to get in Canada and, third, all that he can get from non-scheduled countries, which means the United Kingdom, Italy, France and any of the other countries which produce textiles. That is open to every textile merchant in this country. I am told that Canadian buyer groups are now in the United Kingdom actually buying British textiles.

I do not want to be tiresome about this matter, but I wish to point out that all the minister has said sounds very well and I know it is all true. But it does not affect at all the cases I am talking about. It does not. do a single thing for the small man just getting started, who has not been able to get in Canada what the minister has said he was entitled to, and should get in Canada. But the fact is that many of them were getting nothing. Therefore that man is now expected to carry on with the 32 per cent, and he cannot do so.

Now, because of exchange difficulties, and because we would like to go back to our traditional market abroad, the quotas were framed to cut down drastically our textile imports from the United States and allow the greatest freedom to import textiles from the United Kingdom in the hope of re-establishing the traditional pre-war pattern of textile imports.

Unless we are prepared to buy textiles from the United Kingdom, our whole economy and the whole trade position of the world will get into an awful mess, so that it is an excellent thing to encourage our trade with Britain. It is only fair to the United Kingdom that our textile trade with them be re-established; and it is up to us, other things being equal, or even if they are not equal, to do what we can to establish that industry. When we look at the advertisements of the big stores in the newspapers we see prices of imported British goods which I for one do not understand. I should like to know how it is that these goods are so expensive. I cannot understand why prices are mostly prohibitive, and how we can save United States dollars by spending so much more money to buy these goods. I find it extraordinary. A good hat costs $15-a soft felt hat-when imported from the United Kingdom, and other goods correspondingly. Textiles are most expensive. How is the [DOT]Canadian economy to buy goods that are so much higher than normal prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As regards leather goods and rubber goods, the quota percentage there is 68 per cent, and that is arrived at in this way. Pre-war imports in 1937-39, from scheduled countries, $3,398,000. Imports from

scheduled countries, base period 1946-47, were $9,739,000. Twice 200 per cent of $3,398,000, or $6,000,000 odd, is 68 per cent of the last year's figure, so that there is a direct relationship there. You take 200 per cent of your pre-war average and establish the percentage which that dollar figure represents of last year's imports, and that percentage is the quota for the past year.

And that percentage
quota may differ with each commodity?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has the effect of tending to re-establish the pattern of trade as it existed pre-war.
I would ask the minister, who is always so courteous and obliging, to tell me something in answer to my question about high prices of imported goods when there is little duty on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What kind of goods?

Take a hat, for example. My hon. friend knows that a good hat such as we paid $7 and $8 for before, an imported British or French hat, now costs $15. How is it that when the pound is so low and the franc has been devalued, we in Canada have to pay so much for these imported goods? That is the first part of the question. The second part is this: where is the economy when we spend twice as much to pay for these goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I can give a satisfactory answer to that. I suppose the reason that the price of the English or the French hat is higher is that there has been a greater increase in costs, including wages, in those countries than there has been here. It is so long since I bought a hat that I do not know about the prices. One was given to me last year by a grateful constituent, so that I have not had to buy a hat for some time, but I have no doubt that they do cost $15. As to the second part of the question, the advantage in buying goods from non-scheduled countries, if such goods are at a competitive price, is that they do not involve the expenditure of United States dollars which we need badly, while we are fairly well supplied with sterling or francs as the case may be.
Would the minister be willing to add to those reasons the fact that the pound is much too high in relation to the Canadian dollar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a matter on which we do not need to express an opinion.

We should make hats with pounds. They would be much cheaper.

In view of the minister's statement, I think it might be well to ask this question. Take quotas with scheduled countries. It may not be very practical; but suppose it were possible, by reason of a three-cornered arrangement, to buy goods beyond the quota say from Switzerland, without the use of hard currency, would there be an objection to that?

The hon. gentleman, who is a financier of fame, knows very well that at the present time the currency of Switzerland ranks top high, and moreover it is at a premium. That is one country in the world where the United States dollar is not worth 100 cents. It is not at par but below par. Let us discuss this question of trade in an effort to understand the matter. I still come back to my point that our trade with the United States is real trade, that our trade with Switzerland would be real trade, but our trade with many other countries will not be real trade unless we permit barter, and it is impossible to practise that method if the government intervenes. It might be between two governments, between two individuals, and between two companies, but it cannot be done between two individuals when the government intervenes, and that is the reason for our difficulty with Great Britain. It is due to the fact that the government of Great Britain is the obstacle in the way of trade with that country, just as the United States dollar is the obstacle in the way of our trade with that country.
I know what the hon. member is trying to say, but he is not right.

Opinions are free, but my hon. friend did not agreee with me at the time we were supplying money to buy these things. I thought that process was entirely wrong. He was then full of conviction as he is now, but he was entirely wrong and unfortunately I was right. I do not say that to boast that I am always right, but I remember my hon. friend has been wrong much oftener than I have been, especially in this matter.

Before we leave textiles I

speechtext: The figure I was mentioning of ten times was in cotton yardage. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is an interesting suggestion. I have been answering so many questions here today that my brain is not clicking now as clearly as it might.

I want to make something clear to the hon. member for Temiscouata, if that is possible. I want to agree with him when he says that when governments interfere with barter, it makes things difficult. With that part of his statement I agree. But I do not agree with his statement that the British government is to blame for what is going on now under this bill. This government in Canada is to blame for applying the non-discrimination clauses of the Geneva trade agreements when dealing with these restrictions, not the British government.

Well, I am not going to argue at full length about this, because I would be discussing the principle of the bill. I have been called to order too often and supposedly for discussing the principle of it. I will wait for some other time to do so again. I will tell my hon. friend that it is unfortunate that members who do not belong to the C.C.F. group know the dealings of the present British government better than they themselves do, although they are their own kin. I will say that if Churchill has been right once, it was when he called them a bunch of incompetents, and I will laud again the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have given consideration to it. This concern went into business only after July 1. It was in business for only a month or two before this regulation came in. As such, of course, it is not eligible for quota. The only people who are eligible are those who were importing during the base period ended June 30, 1947.
As I pointed out the other night, there is a special exception for returned soldiers, but unfortunately this company is only half owned by a veteran, the other half, I am told, being

owned by his brother-in-law, who is not a veteran. While I have every sympathy in the circumstances, after careful consideration it was felt that exception could not be made in this case.

When this discussion was up before, I asked the minister if consideration would be given to this company as a new company, because it was only half veteran-owned. When this legislation was introduced a question was asked and the minister assured the house at that time that consideration would be given to new businesses. New businesses, in spite of the fact that they had not been importing goods in the period immediately prior to the imposition of the regulations, would be given a quota. The same would apply, of course, to veterans who had established new businesses.
It is quite true, as the minister has just said, that this business is only half veteran-owned, the other half being owned by his brother-in-law. But if this veteran is to be cut off, because the business is not entirely veteran-owned, I think he should at least be given consideration on the ground that it is a new business. It should certainly be given consideration on that ground because, as I say, it is the only Canadian company in this business. These people are trying to build up an industry in Canada. The effect of this quota as it is working at the present time, so far as I can see, will be to put these people out of business and to give the entire business to a large United States concern operating a subsidiary in this country.
Surely this legislation should be flexible enough to look after the needs of a small company at that time. Surely it is not to be ground down so rigidly that a small Canadian company just getting into operation when these regulations came into force will be forced out of business, in favour of a large United States concern, just because the regulation happens to read, "must have been in business before this date" or "must have had a quota", or something else.
I would ask the minister to give the matter serious consideration, on the basis, as I say, of a new business, rather than from the point of view of the red tape of regulations which have been laid down governing this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We discussed this matter thoroughly the other night. This is a new business, it is true. Provision is not made and cannot be made in these regulations for giving everyone who is in a new business after June 30 a quota. The system would be impossible to work. You must establish a date-line,

and the date-line for those who were entitled to a quota applies to those who were in business prior to June 30, 1947. There has been one exception, and that is, we have reserved a special place for veterans.
We have got along in this country for seventy-five or eighty years without this importing firm bringing in bowling balls from the United States. They only want to do business as importers. They are not making bowling balls and, sympathetic as I am for their position, it is comparable with that of a great many others in new businesses across the country who got into business as importers after July 1, 1947.
Unfortunately, under the existing circumstances, they have to find a source of imports other than from the United States. As I say, we went into this case thoroughly. It was discussed the other night. I have examined it again since that time and I can only say, with reluctance but with firmness, that it is not possible to give this firm a quota under these regulations.
I submit with respect, that the minister does not yet understand this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, if I do not I have had the greatest opportunity to learn it, from stem to gudgeon.

I know the minister has had a lot of correspondence on it. Nevertheless I think he does not yet understand. He seems to think that this is purely an importing business, that it is only importing billiard and bowling balls. That is not so. It is essentially a manufacturing firm. It is manufacturing billiard tables, billiard cues and billiard racks. It is manufacturing bowling alleys. As a necessary part of its billiard and bowling alley manufacturing business it must have bowling balls and billiard balls to supply its customers. The minister seems to think all that is concerned here is a little company which has started up to import balls from the United States or from whereever it can get them, and this only within recent times. But that is not the case. This is a manufacturing company which actually has about thirty-five people working for it, chiefly artificers, cabinet makers and people of that sort. It is a frightful thing to deny these people their source of supply.

speechtext:
I told the hon. member for Calgary East the other night that hard cases make bad law. When you try to make exceptions to a thing like this you get into trouble. I have been criticized here for having this legislation drawn in such a way as to
