Then we endeavoured to get at least the saving that was estimated, and naturally we tried to do even a bit better. As we got down to individual items and came to discuss them with the manufacturers, we have been able to do at least as well as we anticipated so far, and in some cases very much better. If we can do better we are not bound by the first idea we had, as my hon. friend thinks we should be. He thinks it is a very bad job if you are not bound by something you thought you could do a few months ago, but we take that chance and just do the best we can.
For the first time I think the minister is beginning to make a start at answering my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: You understand that, do you?
Oh, yes, I do; and if we stay at it long enough I think we may both understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The minister was stating the obvious.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce can look after himself, so just leave it to him. Well, with considerable difficulty we have reached the point where the minister admits there was an objective, and he has told us they were able to do 100 per cent better than the objective they had in connection with the motorcar industry, so it would seem to me that it was a very poor objective to begin with, but we shall let that pass. However, we still do not have the slightest idea of how that objective was arrived at. You just told us you thought it would be a good idea to tiy to save 135,000,000. Would you' tell us what the imports were last year; and do not tell me they are on record somewhere, because I would like them now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That question has been answered two or three times.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The three companies that manufacture in Canada imported about $71,000,000 in parts.
That is, complete cars and parts?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
No, just parts. Just calm down, now; your specialty is gold, you know. Is that clear; does that answer the question?

Now I suppose you want the value of the imported cars; is that right? Is that of interest, too?

I want to know just how you arrived at this $35,000,000 you were going to save. I assume there was some kind of plan in this; I am
giving you that much credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We were just saying-
I would ask hon. members to maintain the decorum of the chamber and address the Chair, even in asking questions.
I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman; I thought I was doing so.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I was advised by my legal friend sitting beside me that I was being cross-examined by probably the least expert cross-examiner who ever sat in the house, but I told him the excuse was that you were not a cross-examiner but a banker. However, we shall get on. Imports of finished cars, in addition to the $71,000,000, were about $41,000,000; that is, imports from hard currency countries.
I understand from the minister, if my addition is good-and if it is not he will correct me-that the total was about $112,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes, about that.
Then you set out to cut it down by $35,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
And I understand it was cut down by $75,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I have not mentioned the exports there.
I am quite ready to let the minister take his time in telling the story, but we want to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Of course there are also the earnings from exports to which I have just referred. I put all this on Hansard somewhere, but it is a little difficult to gather it together from memory. I thought I could pick a few figures from the air which were not bad, but to take the exports and add in the earnings is a little difficult. I shall be glad to get the analysis, however, and show where the saving of $75,000,000 arises.

Foreign Exchange Conservation

I would remind the minister that this is at least the third time he has said he has not the figures here. The point is that the minister does not take the trouble to come here prepared to answer our legitimate questions, so we will just stay here and keep asking questions, though he will be annoyed and -perhaps we shall be annoyed too.

Yesterday the hon. member for Maple Creek coined, I think inadvertently, the word "mathemagician". As I listened to the .Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario discussing this item, which deals with moving [DOT]picture film negatives, and then get involved in statistics concerning automobiles-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I was just going to ask what item we were on.

-I believe they are both "mathemagicians." I should like to ask a simple question on the item, and I would appreciate a simple answer, if the minister can give it to me. This item, which involves the import of films from scheduled countries amounting to some ten or twelve million dollars, according to the minister, I presume takes into consideration the fact that there are imports from non-scheduled countries. Is this item in schedule III to make it possible to secure an adequate influx of British films to Canada, which I presume were not in great abundance or great demand in Canada during the period prior to 1939? Could the minister give us the picture as to what effect this will have on the British film industry and also on the United States film industry, because I believe that is what the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario started to get at.
I have not got into the films yet at all.
But that is what we are all trying to get at.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is not the present intention to interfere with the distribution of films in Canada. British films come here freely. They have their own distribution in their own theatres, as the United States films have; and films continue to come in as in the past. We are trying to get a reasonable offset for the drain of United States dollars resulting from the importation of United States films. As I say, I think that we are working out a transaction which will represent a reasonable quid pro quo. I am not able to announce it here, because all the details are not worked out; and to give part of the story might not be helpful in closing the transaction.

In view of the fact that this is entirely in the minister's hands, I presume he is making provision to protect non-scheduled country exports to Canada. This refers to motion picture negatives which, I presume, are the commercial films. They are one and one-eighth inches in width.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
That is the thing concerning which we should like some assurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We are not putting any obstacles in their way. We would, of course, welcome more British films. But all I can say. is that I do not know how much I can cultivate it. However, I am not putting any obstacles in their way.
And with respect to the importation of United States films, the minister can assure the committee that it is proposed to attach certain conditions which will be beneficial to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes, that is right.

In connection with the moving picture film business, it does seem strange that we went all through schedules I and II and that we purposely took the prewar pattern of trade and made it possible for Great Britain to send over as much in goods as she could, because they owed us lots of money and we needed their products. Now we come to films and we find that the government have not followed that formula at all. I think the committee is entitled to some of the reasoning behind this. We know that the United States film industry was very hard hit by the action of the United Kingdom, which had the same problem we had, namely the shortage of United States dollars. They cut United States films down drastically. But we followed the opposite course and put no limitation upon them at all.
It is hard to criticize too severely until we know what the quid pro quo is. However, I think we should point out some of the things that are in our minds at least. It does seem to some of us to savour of United States domination. The last thing the United States government wishes to do just now is to do anything to hurt the United States film industry to any greater extent than has been done by the United Kingdom restriction of imports of United States films.
I think the government should give some very good reason why we have followed such a different cotirse in respect to this one product, namely United States films, from the course we have followed in connection with
Foreign Exchange Conservation

every other product normally imported into this country. And because we are chronically short of United States dollars, even in normal times, it would seem to me that no harm would be occasioned if we were to give a little lift to the British film industry here at the present time as against the number of United States films which come in. They have the great advantage over British films because of our way of life and our being adjacent to the United States. And when we are doing everything we can, or making it possible for the British people to pay for the things we want to sell to them-for instance wheat, which we have no place else to sell-I think the committee should be given the reason why we differentiate so completely when it comes to films. Why do we make such a difference between films and other matters?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The film industry does not, in 'our opinion, lend itself to quotas.
The United Kingdom did it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They practically prohibited them by putting a 75 per cent tax on the receipts. And the result is that the United States industry stopped shipping. I have not noticed any indication that it has helped the British film industry one iota. In fact, they are talking about unemployment in the film industry; I was just reading about that tonight. However, if my hon. friend can suggest any way of helping the British films to come here, I shall be very glad to consider it. But I cannot think of any way, except to go over there and buy them, and bring them out. They are entirely free to come into this market.
When you cannot eat lettuce you eat something else; when you cannot get United States films you receive British films.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Probably my hon. friend does not go very often to the moving pictures, but I understand that people do have their tastes in films. If we can give them what they want, the idea is not to impose unnecessary conditions on them. We will not disturb the habits of the film goers if we can get a quid pro quo which is equally valuable. I do not know why my hon. friend should object; be does not go to the movies.
I did not say I do not go.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: You talk like a man who does not.
Oh, not at all. I always talk for the public interest.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Minister of Trade and Commerce put up the argument that we should not disturb" the habits of film goers. This afternoon and the other night when we were arguing for the importation of fresh vegetables, and when we then did not want the habits of Canadians upset, we were told we had to save United States dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend left out just one word. I said "unnecessarily". I said if we can get a quid pro quo without disturbing it, then that is a better solution. When I speak of a quid pro quo I mean getting a very good share of value for that $10,000,000. I think perhaps in commercial value it might be close to $10,000,000. But I would rather have something valuable for the money, and give our people their films, than I would simply stop films and have no money to buy valuable things.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is because we wanted something for them that we asked for fresh fruit and vegetables.

I was just about to say what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just said. It is difficult to understand the policies of this government because there really does not seem to be very much rhyme or reason in what they do.
But what I rose to say was that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. member for Rosedale ought to see some films, and I would suggest that they should see British films. They are excellent. I am not a movie fan; but occasionally when I get tired listening to members of parliament I take in a movie.
Mickey Mouse?

I would suggest that they should see some British films, and then they would be in a position to recommend them to their friends. In my opinion, those I have seen are far superior to the Hollywood brand.
That is my contention.
To get away from the movies. I should like to get back to real life for a moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: May I ask what item we are discussing, and where the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario gets his position.
I will explain that.

We are discussing tariff item ex 238a, with respect to cinematograph or moving picture film negatives one and one-eighth of an inch in width or over.

Foreign Exchange Conservation

May I be permitted to say a word? When we were discussing permits earlier in the bill, if I am not mistaken the Minister of Finance said that the proper place to discuss permits in general, as to the way they are being given, would be when we came to schedule III. I wish to see whether I am right or not in my understanding. I wish to discuss the general question of permits, and I understand that this is the place to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is all right if my hon. friend wishes to discuss permits. But if he wishes to discuss the figures on automobiles or machinery he should do so under the proper item.

I shall bow to the ruling of the Chair. When we are talking about permits, first of all let us consider the subject. We are talking about the saving of United States dollars, and we are 'talking about this extraordinary procedure which we have to resort to, because of certain things which have happened; and we do not need to discuss them now. But one of the things which is essential in discussing these permits is to know how they are being used, and the whole basis upon which they are arrived' at.
When we were on schedules I and II the Minister of Finance very fairly and properly explained the basis upon which this is being done. I think it is nonsense for us to consider these items one by one when we have not had an explanation of the whole basis governing the giving of these permits. Now is the time for us to get figures from the minister as well as an explanation as to how this is worked out. The other night I brought up the question to the minister, and he explained to us that he had made regulations in connection with the automobile industry. I have those regulations; I have read them and' I was bold enough to say to the minister that they read pretty sensibly. But I wanted' to know and still want to know-if this is not the right place to get it, we can get it some place else-and I suggest that now is the time to find out whether there is any rhyme or reason to this system under which permits are being given. The minister has made it very difficult. After a couple of Slips of memory, he finally got down to the point where he explained what they bad in the automobile industry. He has never told us how they worked it out. He just told us that was 105 per cent up. I am never very much impressed by people who figure out this sort of thing themselves. They always try to make it easy for themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Item 438a covens automobiles. If my hon. friend can exercise his patience that long I shall be prepared to give him all the data he is now asking for. But in the meantime I wish he would not talk about automobiles.
I am talking about permits.
Are you speaking on the point of order raised by the minister?

I am speaking on the point of order raised by the minister. I am talking about permits and I used automobiles merely as an illustration. I want an explanation from the minister of how the whole business of permits under schedule III is approached. Has he an objective that he is working for? He has told us more or less that he has one in the automobile industry, and I want to know what his other objectives are. I want to know the amount of United States exchange he is allowing himself in connection with the steel industry, the motor industry and other industries. I want to know what figure we are dealing with. We are dealing with hundreds of millions of the money of the people of Canada. What the minister is trying to do is to juggle this thing along and have it left so that we have not the slightest idea of what figure he has in mind, and so that- there will be nothing in the world that we can hold him to later on. I ask you Mr. Chairman, to rule that this is a proper time to discuss the basis of the permits under schedule III and that there is no other time to discuss it.

I must rule that the question of permits would come up under schedule III, but at the same time the discussion of permits would have to be generalized in connection with the single item. We are discussing item ex 238a, and it would be in order to discuss permits for cinematograph or moving picture films and nothing else. There will be an opportunity of speaking about permits for automobiles later on. That is my ruling.
Mr. MACDONNELL .(Muskoka-Ontario): I bow to your ruling, but I think it will complicate matters. It means that under each item we have to ask the minister what his objective is in the matter of United States exchange and how he is getting along with it. I think it will waste a lot of time but I bow to your ruling.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
May I say generally about permits that I have absolutely no authority

Foreign Exchange Conservation
to issue any permit, because the official opposition has kept rolling this bill over since the middle of January and not putting me in a position of authority whereby I can issue permits. If this bill passes, then I can begin issuing permits, but if you ask me now about permits I must say that I am not doing any business.
I am sure that, on reflection, the minister will want to withdraw those remarks. If he intends to blame the opposition-
He said the official opposition.
The minister cannot blame any member of the opposition for the government's failure to formulate and enunciate a clear policy.
Again I must remind hon. members that we are on item 238a. Shall the item carry?
No.

I want to say something about the minister's last remark. Mr. Chairman, you purported to call us back to a particular item, and then the minister made certain remarks which constitute a grave reflection on one side of the house. If the remarks of those of us who want to say something by way of correcting the minister are ruled out of order, then certainly you should have ruled the minister out of order before he made remarks of that kind.
I should like to recall, for the benefit of the minister, certain facts which obviously he has forgotten in connection with the matter of bringing into effect the provisions of schedule III or the permit set-up under this whole scheme. When we were here in December the minister announced to the house that there would be some delay with respect to the whole permit system, that he was not going to bring it into effect until February 1. Then, in due course there was another announcement deferring the date. Those announcements had absolutely nothing to do with the passing of the bill; the minister gave quite different reasons for his action at that time. What he is now trying to do is to use something that has nothing whatever to do with this present issue before the committee, to drag that out as a red herring to cover up the fact that this whole program is such that the government does not know what it is doing or where it is going.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Do not take yourself too
seriously.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Sit down, my boy.
Sit down, you are too young.
Any more of those slapstick remarks from the ministerial benches will not contribute anything either to the decorum of the chamber or to the celerity of the proceedings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well put.
When the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, Trade and Commerce and everything else, the jack of all trades in the cabinet-
Order.
-undertakes to make remarks intended to disparage those in the house who do not happen to have his years-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Shame.

I want to say to him that I think references of that kind do not reflect any credit on him. There are a great many people sitting around him, younger men, who are not getting the chance they should in this house, simply because those who occupy the treasury benches do all the talking and do not give the young men behind them a chance to show their real ability.
I would ask members of the committee to come down to earth and consider the item we have before us.

That can certainly be done if the ministers will refrain from these remarks with which they load up Hansard, simply because they sit beside the Hansard reporter. Remarks like that reflect no credit on the chamber or on the minister.

On a point of order, I believe the hon. gentleman is exhausting his steam power. I do not think he has the right, under the rules of the house, to cast reflections on or to impute motives to a minister. He is saying that the minister does all the talking because he wants to crush or squash, or whatever the word is, the backbenchers behind him, who are actually all heartily behind the minister. I say that he is imputing motives to the minister which he has no right to do, and I ask the hon. member to retrieve and to withdraw his remarks.

Is it not a fact that the importation of British films is conditioned

Foreign Exchange Conservation
upon the ownership of theatres in Canada? Is the number of British films that we can bring in not strictly limited by the ownership of the outlets?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I would doubt that very much. I think if we got British films in proportion to British outlets as compared with United States owned outlets we would have far more British films. The Odeon people own almost as many theatres as Paramount and we do not get nearly as many British films.
The minister holds the balance in connection with films coming from the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No, I hold no balance. I do not disturb in the slightest the distribution of films.
The minister must exercise some discretion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Not a bit.
How much is to be saved by the plan that is not yet in existence?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Not very much.

If we are to have in the functioning of these various schedules what I might call side deals such as the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests he is having with the United States movie industry, I would close by reminding the Minister of Finance that I gave him what I thought was a worthwhile side deal on how to trade cattle for cabbages, and I did not even get the courtesy of an answer from him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do not miss your train; Toronto needs you.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-306. Marble, sawn or sand rubbed, not polished; granite, sawn; paving blocks of stone; flagstone and building stone, other than marble or granite, sawn on not more than two sides.

I am interested in these four items dealing with building stone. I have had some communication, with the assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce with respect to importations of some of these items from Wisconsin, and I wish to express here my appreciation of the expeditious way in which they looked after that business.
But sometimes it so happens that when a substitute stone is available in Canada for a building, particularly a public building, the substitute does not fit into the architectural 5849-95	.
pattern, and consideration should be given to that feature, particularly when buildings still uncompleted have been a long time under construction prior to the introduction of this bill.
Would the minister indicate just how much money is involved in these four items for building stone? What were our imports prior to the war in the three-year period generally referred to from scheduled and non-scheduled countries? What was the amount imported in 1947 from the same source, and how much does the minister expect to save on these four items by whatever regulations he is about to adopt?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The figures are granite rough, $193,744, from the United States; $697 from Mexico, $3,350 from Italy. Granite sawn, $179,813, of which $71,663 came from the United States, and $90,691 from Sweden, which is also a hard currency country. Granite manufacture, $32,306. Marbie sawn, $104,585, chiefly from the United States, Marble for tombstones, $109,970. Marble manufacturers, $55,712. Those are the principal items, totaling around $1,000,000.

The imports are larger than I expected. In general, we can develop substitutes for most of the items, but not for all of them. I presume the minister is prepared to give the assurance that, where a certain type of stone has been specified by the architects for a public building and it is not readily available in Canada, he will not hold up the building.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If the building is partly completed we would naturally co-operate, but we sincerely hope that large quantities of stone will not be used, because that is not the type of building we are trying to encourage. If limestone is used we would rather have the Canadian product used, but architects are apt to specify Indiana limestone.

A number of schools are now being built in Toronto, and the practice down through the years has been to use Indiana limestone. I understood the minister to give me the assurance the other day that there would be no prohibition of Indiana limestone being brought in to finish buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I think the architect would' have to do a good deal of explaining why he could not use another stone or dispense with stone altogether. In any event, as I explained to my hon. friend, we realize that growing communities must have schools, and we are

Foreign Exchange Conservation

prepared to examine the projects and decide on the basis of the actual project what can and cannot be done.
A few days ago an official was here from Toronto and, I presume, discussed with the department the likelihood of their being able to obtain some kind of stone.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No, he did not mention stone. He talked about steel, and we said that if it was not more than three stories high, reinforced concrete could be used.

It would be foolish to
insist on a school already half built with one type of stone being finished with some other type of stone. The school would be an eyesore to the children. We do not want anything like that.
Item 306 stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would the minister indicate the business for Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall ask the house to allow me to advance one stage a resolution standing in my name to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which will expire at the end of this month, and if the house will agree we might even give the bill its second reading. It is not controversial. The amendment is merely to extend for a further period of three years the act, which has proved reasonably successful. When that is disposed of we shall proceed with Bill No. 3, with which we have been dealing this evening, and if, as I hope, we dispose of that we shall proceed in committee with the resolution relating to the excise tax portion of the emergency program.

speechtext: At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to .standing order.
